What is the Budget and what could be in it?

gist: Labour is considering options to raise funds without increasing income tax, VAT or National Insurance.
Potential measures include higher bank surcharges, gambling taxes, online VAT enforcement and welfare cuts.
The government faces shrinking fiscal headroom alongside pressures from living costs and defence spending.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The government faces a shrinking fiscal buffer, which economists estimate may have fallen from £24bn to £11bn. With manifesto pledges ruling out increases to income tax, VAT, or National Insurance, options to raise revenue include raising the corporation tax surcharge on banks and doubling the tax on electronic gaming machines. Another proposal would make online marketplaces such as Amazon, Ebay and Temu responsible for collecting VAT owed by platform sellers. Reducing welfare spending is also being considered.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Chancellor John Healey needs funds to maintain fiscal rules, support defence spending and assist with the cost of living. The proposed tax measures could raise around £3.5bn annually, though critics highlight potential downsides. Gambling taxes could worsen odds for users, and online sellers might raise consumer prices. Restricting health and disability benefits could push recipients into poverty, while experts caution that required back-to-work support might offset immediate savings.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Chancellor is expected to present the Budget on Wednesday. Any welfare reforms may face political hurdles, following previous backbench revolts over proposed benefit reductions.
